items.question: Do you agree or disagree with the following statement? University students should have a part-time job while they are in school. Use specific reasons and examples to support your opinion.

lv5.text: I agree that university students should have a part-time job. I have two reasons. First, they can earn money. They can pay for books and food. Second, they can learn about work. For example, my friend worked at a café. She learned how to talk to customers. So I agree with this statement.

I disagree with this statement. I think students should focus on studying. First, university classes are difficult. Students need a lot of time to study. Second, a part-time job is tiring. For example, my cousin worked at night. He was always tired in class. So I think students should not work.

lv6.text: I agree that university students should have a part-time job. There are two reasons. First, students can earn their own money. These days, tuition and living costs are very high, so a part-time job can help them pay for books, food, and transportation. Second, they can get real work experience. For example, when I worked at a bakery during university, I learned how to deal with customers and manage my time. This experience helped me a lot when I got my first job. For these reasons, I agree with the statement.

I disagree that university students should have a part-time job. I have two reasons. First, studying is a full-time job for students. Many university classes need a lot of reading and group work, so students don't have enough time to work. Second, working can hurt their grades. For example, when I worked at a restaurant in my first year, I was always tired and my grades went down. After I quit, my grades got much better. So I think students should focus on their studies.

lv7.text: I agree that university students should have a part-time job while they are in school. I have two main reasons. First, a part-time job teaches students how to manage money. When students earn their own money, they understand how hard it is to make, so they spend it more carefully. Second, it gives them practical skills that they can't learn in a classroom. For example, during my second year of university, I worked at a convenience store three evenings a week. At first, it was difficult to balance work and study, but I learned how to plan my schedule and handle difficult customers calmly. These skills really helped me later at my internship. Therefore, I strongly believe that working part-time is valuable for university students.

I disagree with the idea that university students should have a part-time job. In my opinion, university is a short and important period, and students should use it to build their future. First of all, a part-time job takes away time that students could spend on more valuable activities, like internships, club activities, or studying for certificates. Also, most part-time jobs for students, such as serving food or working at a store, are not related to their major. For example, my roommate worked at a fast-food restaurant for two years, but that experience didn't help him at all when he applied for jobs in engineering. For these reasons, I think students should focus on their studies instead.
phrases: I disagree with the idea that

lv8.text: Personally, I agree that university students should have a part-time job, as long as it doesn't take too much time away from their studies. The main reason is that a part-time job helps students become more independent and responsible. When you have a boss, coworkers, and a fixed schedule, you learn very quickly that other people are depending on you. I experienced this myself. In my third year, I worked as an English tutor for a middle school student twice a week. Preparing lessons every week forced me to manage my time much better, and I actually got better grades that semester because I stopped wasting my free time. On top of that, the experience helped me figure out what kind of career I wanted. So overall, I think a part-time job can be one of the most valuable parts of university life.

I can see why some people think a part-time job is a good idea, but personally, I disagree with this statement. University is probably the only time in your life when you can focus completely on learning, and I think students should make the most of it. When students work fifteen or twenty hours a week, something has to give, and it's usually sleep or study time. I saw this happen to a close friend of mine. She worked evening shifts at a hotel front desk during her second year, and by the end of the semester she had dropped one of her major courses because she simply couldn't keep up. Of course, if a student really needs the money, that's a different story. But generally, I believe students are better off investing their time in their education.

items.question: Which do you think is better for completing team projects: working together in the same office, or working remotely from home? Use specific reasons and examples to support your opinion.

lv5.text: I think working together in the office is better. I have two reasons. First, we can talk face to face. It is fast and easy. Second, we can solve problems together. For example, in my team, we had a problem last month. We met in a meeting room and fixed it in one hour. So I prefer the office.

I think working remotely is better for team projects. First, I can save time. I don't need to take the bus to work. Second, I can focus at home. The office is noisy. For example, my friend works at home. She says she finishes her work faster. So I like working remotely.

lv6.text: I think working together in the office is better for team projects. There are two reasons. First, communication is much faster. If I have a question, I can just walk to my coworker's desk and ask. Online, I have to wait for an answer. Second, it is easier to build a good relationship with team members. For example, last year my team worked on a big project in the office. We had lunch together every day, and we became close. Because of that, we worked well as a team. For these reasons, I prefer the office.

In my opinion, working remotely is better for team projects. I have two reasons. First, people can work at their best time. Some people focus better in the morning, and some people focus better at night. Second, we don't waste time on long meetings. For example, my team uses an online chat and a shared document. We write our ideas there, so we only meet once a week for thirty minutes. This saves a lot of time. So I think working remotely is better.

lv7.text: I believe working together in the same office is better for team projects. I have two main reasons. First, it's much easier to share ideas when everyone is in the same room. In a face-to-face meeting, people can react right away, and one idea often leads to another. Second, problems can be solved more quickly. For example, when I was working on a product launch last year, our designer noticed a mistake in the plan. Because we were sitting next to each other, we fixed it in ten minutes. If we had been working from home, it probably would have taken a whole day of emails. For these reasons, I think the office is the better choice for team projects.
phrases: one idea often leads to another

lv7.text: In my opinion, working remotely is better for team projects. First of all, it gives team members more time to focus. In an office, people are often interrupted by phone calls and small talk. At home, it's quieter, so they can finish their part of the project faster. Second, remote work makes it easier to work with people in different places. For example, last semester I did a group project with classmates who lived in three different cities. We used video calls and a shared online folder, and we finished the project a week early. Without remote tools, that would have been impossible. Therefore, I think working remotely is the better option.

lv8.text: Personally, I think working together in the same office is better for team projects, even though remote work has become very common. The main reason is that teamwork depends on trust, and trust is much easier to build in person. When you see your coworkers every day, you notice when someone is struggling, and you can offer help before a small problem becomes a big one. I learned this from experience. At my previous job, our team was fully remote for about a year, and although everyone was working hard, we kept missing small details because nobody wanted to bother each other with questions. After we moved back to the office, those misunderstandings almost disappeared, and our projects started finishing on schedule. So overall, I believe sharing the same space makes a team work more smoothly.

I'd argue that working remotely is actually better for team projects, as long as the team has clear rules. The biggest advantage is flexibility. When people can choose where and when they work, they tend to be more productive and less stressed. For example, my current team is spread across two different cities, and we work almost entirely online. At first, I was worried that communication would suffer, but we set up a simple system: a short video call every morning, and everything else goes into a shared project board. Because every decision is written down, nobody misses important information, and new members can catch up quickly. Honestly, our projects run more smoothly now than when we all shared an office. So I'd say remote work is the better choice.

lv7.text: I believe taking an in-person class is a better way to learn a new skill. The biggest reason is that you can get feedback right away. Also, studying with other people keeps me motivated, because I don't want to fall behind the others. Therefore, I strongly prefer in-person classes for learning new skills.

I think watching online videos is a better way to learn a new skill. First, it's much more flexible. I work full-time, so it's hard for me to attend a class at a fixed time every week. With videos, I can learn whenever I have free time, like late at night or on weekends. Second, there's a huge variety of content. lv8.text: Personally, I think taking an in-person class is the better option, especially for skills that involve your body, like sports or cooking. Of course, classes have their benefits, like meeting other learners, but for busy people, videos are simply more practical and much easier to fit into a daily routine.

items.question: Which is more important when choosing a job: a high salary or good relationships with coworkers? Give specific reasons and examples to support your opinion.

lv5.text: I think good coworkers are more important. I have two reasons. First, I see my coworkers every day. Second, work is easier when people help me. For example, at my part-time job, my coworkers were very kind. I was happy at work. So I think coworkers are more important.

I think a high salary is more important. First, I need money to live. Rent and food are expensive. Second, I want to save money for the future. For example, my friend got a job with a high salary. He bought a car last year. So I choose a high salary.

lv6.text: In my opinion, good relationships with coworkers are more important than a high salary. There are two reasons. First, I spend more time with my coworkers than with my family on weekdays, so a friendly team makes every day better. Second, good coworkers help me learn faster. For example, at my first job, a senior coworker taught me how to use our sales program, and I got used to my work in just two weeks. For these reasons, I think coworkers matter more.

I think a high salary is more important when choosing a job. First, money gives me more choices in life. I can travel, take classes, and help my parents. Second, relationships can change, because people often move to other teams or companies. But a salary stays with me. For example, my cousin left a friendly company for a job with a higher salary. Now she can save money every month, and she is much less stressed. That's why I prefer a high salary.

lv7.text: Personally, I think good relationships with coworkers are more important than a high salary. The first reason is stress. Even if the pay is great, going to work every day feels terrible when people don't get along. The second reason is growth. When coworkers trust each other, they share tips and give honest feedback, so everyone improves faster. For example, I worked at a small design company a few years ago. The salary wasn't very high, but my team always helped each other with deadlines, and I learned more there than anywhere else. Looking back, I'd choose a team like that again. So, for me, coworkers come first.

I'd say a high salary is more important, especially at the start of a career. First of all, a good salary lets you pay off student loans and start saving early, which reduces a lot of stress. On top of that, salary is something you can actually compare before you accept a job, while relationships with coworkers are hard to predict. For instance, my friend chose a company because the interviewers seemed friendly, but half of his team quit within six months. If he had chosen the higher-paying offer, he would at least have had financial security. That's why I'd focus on the salary first.

lv8.text: Honestly, I believe good relationships with coworkers matter more than a high salary in the long run. To begin with, we spend around forty hours a week at work, and a tense atmosphere can make even a well-paid job feel exhausting. A raise might make you happy for a month, but daily conflicts wear you down for years. Moreover, supportive coworkers can actually boost your career. They introduce you to new projects, cover for you when you're sick, and give you honest feedback. I experienced this myself when I joined a marketing team where everyone shared ideas openly. My salary was average, but I was promoted within two years because my teammates recommended me for a major project. So if I had to choose, I'd pick a great team over a bigger paycheck, because a good team often helps the paycheck grow later anyway.

While good coworkers are important, I'd argue that a high salary should come first when choosing a job. The biggest reason is that a salary affects every part of your life, not just the hours you spend at the office. It decides where you can live, how much you can save, and whether you can support your family. Another reason is that relationships at work are unpredictable. Your favorite manager might move to another branch next month, and a new team member could completely change the atmosphere. A contract, on the other hand, is something you can rely on. My older brother is a good example. He turned down a friendly startup for a better-paying job at a large company, and that extra income allowed him to buy his first apartment three years earlier than he expected. That's why I'd prioritize the salary.
